STRUCTURED DATA DRIFT CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Does your page's JSON-LD actually say what the page says?

Paste a page's HTML and see every FAQPage, HowTo, Article/BlogPosting/NewsArticle, Product, LocalBusiness/Organization, or Review claim in its JSON-LD, checked word for word against the page's own visible text — with the exact character where it drifted when it doesn't match. Google's structured-data guidelines require FAQPage and HowTo content to be visible on the page; AI answer engines go further and read JSON-LD as ground truth when they summarize a page. Either way, a mismatch means the markup is describing a page that no longer exists.

Nothing is uploaded. The HTML you paste is parsed in this browser and never leaves your device.

1. Paste the page's HTML

2. What the JSON-LD claims, checked against the page

ClaimStatusWhere it diverges

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file — and it can check every page in a build in one pass:

node cli.mjs check dist/index.html                     # one page, human-readable
node cli.mjs check dist/index.html --json                # machine-readable
node cli.mjs check dist/**/*.html                         # every page a shell glob expands
find dist -name '*.html' | xargs node cli.mjs check       # or from a build's output tree
node cli.mjs check dist/index.html --strict                # also fail on malformed JSON-LD

Get cli.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install. It reads only the local files you name: no network call, ever. Exits 1 if any claim diverges, so it works as a CI step after a static-site build.

What's checked, per schema type

TypeFields checked

Only textual claims a visitor can read and verify by eye — never opaque numeric or URL fields (ratingValue, priceCurrency, image, and so on), which this tool has no opinion on. LocalBusiness/Organization subtype coverage is a curated list plus a suffix heuristic, stated plainly as non-exhaustive rather than presented as complete.

More: why Google requires this for FAQPage and HowTo, and how AI answer engines make it matter for every other type too. See also: how this differs from Google's Rich Results Test, and how this differs from checking it by eye.

Common questions

Why does this matter for FAQPage and HowTo specifically?

Google's structured data guidelines say FAQPage and HowTo markup must describe content that is visible to a visitor on the page itself. Markup that describes text nobody can see is treated as unreliable, and Google's documentation says a page misusing it may lose the rich result entirely. Every other type this tool checks can drift the same way; those two are simply where Google has said so in writing.

Why would JSON-LD and page copy ever disagree?

Someone edits the visible copy and forgets the JSON-LD, or edits the JSON-LD and forgets the copy. Both are hand-authored text living in different parts of the same file, so nothing forces them to stay in sync, and no build step here catches it unless something like this tool checks.

Is this an SEO audit or a ranking guarantee?

No. It is a deterministic string comparison between two things already in the page you pasted: what the JSON-LD claims and what the visible text says. A clean result means those two texts agree, nothing more. It is not a Search Console substitute, it does not check whether your markup is eligible for a rich result, and it makes no promise about rankings or traffic.

Is my page content uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page parses the HTML you paste entirely in your own browser and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads only local files — no network call, ever.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not SEO, legal, or marketing advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. It reports whether a JSON-LD claim's exact text is present in the page's own visible copy — nothing more. It is not a Search Console substitute, not a ranking guarantee, and not a determination that your structured data is eligible for any rich result. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The HTML you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also worth a pass over the same page: AI Crawler Access Check checks whether your robots.txt actually lets AI crawlers reach the page whose structured data this tool is checking — a different failure mode in the same "can an AI system actually see and trust this page" question.

Same "does the doc still match the code" shape, different pair: .env.example Drift Check diffs a repo's example environment file against what the code actually reads, instead of a page's JSON-LD against its own visible text.

One layer over on the Shopping side: Merchant Feed Check checks the separate Google Merchant Center / Meta Catalog feed Shopping results actually read — the other representation of a product Google can pull structured data from and cross-check against.

A different metadata surface on the same page: Social Preview Checker checks a page's Open Graph and Twitter Card tags and its preview image's real pixel dimensions — what a shared link renders as, rather than what a search or AI crawler reads as structured data.

Same "does what search engines read still match what the page claims" question, a different signal: Canonical Tag Checker checks which URL a page's own canonical link tag names as authoritative, instead of whether its JSON-LD text matches its visible copy.

Related: the JSON-LD rich result validator checks that markup has every required property and builds starter markup.

Free and open source. If this saved you some digging, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-checking-it-by-eye.html.text:
← Structured Data Drift Check

Structured Data Drift Check vs. checking it by eye

This page names no specific product or company: "checking it by eye" is view-source plus reading, a generic manual habit anyone with a browser already has, not a competing tool.

Reading a page's <script type="application/ld+json"> block and comparing it by eye against the rendered page genuinely works for the case most people picture when they think about checking this: one short FAQ answer, one matching paragraph, both in view at the same time. That case is real, and it is not what this tool exists to replace. What it replaces is everything past that case — escaped punctuation that reads as ordinary text, a node nested inside another node, more than one <script> block on the page, and a claim long enough that a dropped clause in the middle produces no visual cue at all.

CaseChecking it by eyeThis tool
One short FAQ answer next to its matching paragraph, both in view togetherWorks fine — this is the case the habit is built forAlso passes, the same way, as one of six checked claim types
A JSON-escaped straight quote (\") vs. a curly one rendered on the pageBoth read as an ordinary quote mark scanning past a long raw-text line — no visual difference to noticeSquashes and compares the decoded text directly, so a quote-style mismatch shows up as an exact divergence, not a guess
An em dash written as a plain double hyphen in the JSON-LD, or an HTML entity like —Reads as unremarkable ASCII in the raw source either wayDecodes named and numeric entities before comparing, so the two only match when the actual characters agree
A Review nested inside a Product, or an Organization nested inside an Article's publisher fieldOnly found if the person scanning the script block happens to open that nested object too, past whichever top-level type they were looking forWalks every reachable node in every script block, including @graph arrays and nested fields, so a claim three levels deep is checked the same as a top-level one
A paragraph-length HowTo step or Article descriptionA manual word-for-word comparison across a line-wrap difference — exactly the kind of exhaustive check people get wrong under time pressure, with no signal when they doA deterministic string comparison with no length limit, reporting the exact character where the two diverge
More than one <script type="application/ld+json"> block on the pageEasy to check the one you already scrolled to and skip the othersParses every JSON-LD script block on the page in one pass
Catching drift a future edit introducesA one-time read answers for today; nothing re-checks the page after the next copy editcli.mjs reads local files with no network call and can run as a CI gate on every build

The gap that matters most: escaped text looks identical to decoded text

View-source shows the JSON-LD exactly as authored: a right single quote can be the six literal characters ’ or the escape sequence ’, and an em dash can be typed as two hyphens because it was faster to type than the real character. None of that looks unusual sitting inside a long minified string — there is no red flag, no obviously-wrong shape, just ordinary-looking text. The page's rendered copy, meanwhile, shows the decoded, real character. Two strings that differ by exactly one of these substitutions read as the same thing to someone scanning past them, and stay that way indefinitely, because nothing about a clean-looking read tells you whether you checked the actual characters or the ones your eye auto-corrected on the way past. This tool's decodeEntities step resolves both named and numeric character references before comparing, so a punctuation substitution shows up as a real divergence rather than passing on sight.

The gap that matters second: nesting has no visual marker

Schema.org nodes nest freely — a Review can live inside a Product's review field, an Organization can live inside an Article's publisher field, and a single script block can hold an @graph array of several unrelated top-level nodes. None of that changes how the raw text looks: it is still one long line of nested braces, and there is no highlighting to tell a person scanning it that a checkable claim sits three levels deeper than the type they came looking for. This tool walks every object reachable from every parsed script block — arrays, @graph, and every nested property — so a nested claim is checked the same way a top-level one is, with no dependence on whether a reader happened to open that branch.

When to still read the page yourself

This is a text comparison, not a content review. It has no opinion on whether the copy is accurate, well-written, or eligible for a rich result, and it checks only six schema.org types' textual fields — a claim outside FAQPage, HowTo, Article/BlogPosting/NewsArticle, Product, LocalBusiness/Organization, or Review is invisible to it the same way it would be to a person who never scrolled that far. Judging the substance of the content is still a job for reading it.

Common questions

What does checking JSON-LD against the page by eye actually catch?

It catches the case everyone tests: view-source, find the application/ld+json block, read one short FAQ answer, glance at the matching paragraph on the page, and see they say the same thing. That works fine for a single short claim someone is already looking straight at.

Why does eyeballing miss an entity or escape difference?

The JSON-LD in view-source is a raw, minified, escaped string: a curly right quote is the literal characters \u2019 or an HTML entity, an em dash can be a plain double hyphen, and a straight quote inside the JSON is backslash-escaped as \". None of those render as anything unusual when you read the raw source text — they look like ordinary characters mixed into a long line — so two strings that differ by exactly one of them read as identical to a person scanning past them, while a browser decoding the same page renders visibly different punctuation.

Why does eyeballing miss a nested node?

Real JSON-LD nests: a Review sits inside a Product's review field, an Organization sits inside an Article's publisher field, and an @graph array can hold several unrelated top-level nodes in one script block. Finding every checkable claim means mentally walking that structure without missing a level, for however many script tags the page carries — and a person scanning for the FAQPage block they know is there has no particular reason to also open the Product node three lines below it.

Why is a long claim harder to check by eye than a short one?

A HowTo step or an Article description can run to several sentences. Comparing two paragraph-length strings word for word by eye, across the gap between a minified JSON string and a rendered paragraph with different line wrapping, is exactly the kind of exhaustive comparison people are bad at doing reliably — and unlike a one-line FAQ answer, a single dropped clause in the middle of a long paragraph produces no visual cue that anything is missing.

Does this tool replace reading the page yourself?

No. It only compares text that is already on the page against text that is already in the page's own JSON-LD — it has no opinion on whether the copy is well-written, whether the JSON-LD is eligible for a rich result, or whether a claim outside its six checked types is accurate. Judging the content itself is still a job for reading it.

More: why Google requires structured data to match visible text. See also: how this differs from Google's Rich Results Test.

vs-google-rich-results-test.html.text:
← Structured Data Drift Check

Structured Data Drift Check vs. Google's Rich Results Test

Rich Results Test is Google's own free tool for checking a page's structured data. Paste a URL or a code snippet and it tells you whether the JSON-LD parses correctly and whether the page is eligible for a specific rich result in Google Search — a FAQ rich result, a HowTo carousel, a Product snippet, and so on. It is the closest thing to an authoritative answer for "will Google show this as a rich result", and it is genuinely useful for that question.

That is not this tool's job. Rich Results Test parses your JSON-LD in isolation: it never reads the page's visible, rendered text at all, so it cannot tell you whether what the markup claims still matches what a visitor actually sees. Structured Data Drift Check does exactly that one comparison — it takes JSON-LD that already parses fine and checks, word for word, whether its claims appear in the page's own visible copy, reporting the exact character where the two diverge when they don't.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Is my JSON-LD syntactically valid, and is this page eligible for a specific Google rich result? Rich Results Test — that needs Google's own eligibility rules for each rich result type, which a text-diff tool has no opinion on.
My FAQPage markup is valid and eligible — does it still say what the page's visible text says today? Structured Data Drift Check — paste the page's HTML and get the exact claim, and the exact character, where the two diverge, no signup, nothing leaves your device.
I want to know whether Google will actually show a rich result for this page. Rich Results Test — a text-diff can confirm the words match, it makes no claim about eligibility or ranking.
I want to check this on every page of a build, as a CI gate, without uploading anything to Google. Structured Data Drift Check's CLI — it reads only local files and never makes a network call.

The two are not substitutes. A page that needs to know whether it qualifies for a rich result at all needs Google's own eligibility checker — nothing else can answer that authoritatively. A page whose markup already passes that check, but whose visible copy was edited afterward and the JSON-LD was not, needs the comparison Rich Results Test was never built to make. Running both catches more than either alone: Rich Results Test for eligibility, this tool for whether the eligible markup is still telling the truth.

Common questions

Should I use Structured Data Drift Check or Google's Rich Results Test?

They check different things. Rich Results Test parses your JSON-LD, tells you whether it is syntactically valid, and reports whether the page is eligible for a specific rich result in Google Search. Structured Data Drift Check does not check eligibility at all. It takes JSON-LD that already parses fine and asks a narrower question Rich Results Test does not ask: does the text inside that JSON-LD actually appear, word for word, in the page's own visible content. A FAQPage block can be perfectly valid and fully eligible in Rich Results Test while describing an answer that was rewritten on the page six months ago and never updated in the markup. Rich Results Test has no way to catch that, because it never reads the page's visible text at all.

Does Rich Results Test already catch a mismatch between JSON-LD and visible text?

No. Rich Results Test validates the structured data against schema.org's shape and Google's eligibility rules for a given rich result type. It parses the JSON-LD in isolation and does not compare it against the rendered page content, so a FAQPage answer that no longer matches what a visitor reads on the page will still pass Rich Results Test as valid and eligible. Google's own guidelines say FAQPage and HowTo content must be visible on the page, but Rich Results Test's tool does not enforce that guideline by diffing the two texts — it only checks that the markup itself is well formed.

Is Google's Rich Results Test free?

Yes. Rich Results Test is a free tool at Google's own search.google.com/test/rich-results, with no account required to test a single URL or code snippet. Structured Data Drift Check is also free, with no account, and the two are not competing on price — they check different things and neither replaces the other.

Is this page affiliated with Google?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Google. Google and Rich Results Test are named here only to describe what that tool checks and does not check, based on Google's own public documentation.

More: why Google requires structured data to match visible text.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. why-google-requires-structured-data-to-m.text:
← Back to Structured Data Drift Check

Why Google requires structured data to match visible text

Google's Search Central documentation for the FAQPage and HowTo structured-data types both say the same thing in substance: the markup has to reflect content that is actually on the page and visible to a visitor, not text that exists only inside a <script type="application/ld+json"> block. A page that markets up a question and answer nobody can read is, per that guidance, not eligible for the rich result the markup is meant to earn — and Google's own spam policies treat structured data describing hidden or absent content as a form of misleading markup, not a harmless inaccuracy. This page describes the rule rather than quoting Google's current wording verbatim, because that wording can change without notice; read the current guidance on developers.google.com for the authoritative text.

Why it happens: two authored strings, one source of truth for neither

Nothing about how a page is normally built keeps its visible copy and its JSON-LD in sync. A marketer edits an FAQ answer on the page and never touches the schema. A developer writes the schema once at launch, off the copy as it existed that day, and the copy keeps evolving underneath it. A templating system interpolates the same variable into both places today and a refactor six months later interpolates it into only one. In every case the drift is invisible to a human reader, because nobody reads raw JSON-LD next to rendered copy side by side — which is exactly the comparison this tool automates.

Why this extends past FAQPage and HowTo

Google's written policy names two structured-data types. The underlying reason it exists — markup should describe what is actually on the page — is not specific to either one. An AI system that reads a page's JSON-LD to summarize it, answer a question about it, or decide what to tell a user about a product, business, or review has no equivalent published rule requiring the markup to match what a human visitor sees; it can simply treat the JSON-LD as a structured, pre-parsed statement of fact and repeat it. A Product description, a LocalBusiness address claim in prose, a fabricated-sounding Review body, or an Article headline that no longer matches the page's own <h1> can mislead exactly the same way a stale FAQ answer can — this tool checks all six because the risk is not limited to the two types Google has written a rule about.

What this tool checks, and what it deliberately doesn't

TypeFields checked
FAQPagemainEntity[].name (question), mainEntity[].acceptedAnswer.text (answer)
HowToname, description, step[].name, step[].text
Article / BlogPosting / NewsArticleheadline, description
Productname, description
LocalBusiness / Organization (and common subtypes)name, description
ReviewreviewBody, author.name

Deliberately excluded: numeric and URL fields (ratingValue, priceCurrency, image, url, dates, and so on). Those aren't prose a visitor reads and confirms by eye the way an FAQ answer or a headline is, and a false-positive divergence report on a formatting difference in a number would train a reader to ignore real findings — the same failure mode this portfolio's other checkers avoid by staying narrow.

Wiring it into CI as a gate

Run it against a static build's output directory after every deploy that touches copy or schema:

- name: Check structured data against visible page text
  run: |
    npm run build
    find dist -name '*.html' | xargs node ventures/structured-data-drift-check/cli.mjs check

The command exits non-zero if any claim on any page diverges from that page's own visible text. Add --strict to also fail on a malformed application/ld+json block, which is a different bug this tool notices but does not fail on by default.

Common questions

Where does Google actually say this?

Google's Search Central documentation for both the FAQPage and HowTo structured data types states that the markup must reflect the main content of the page, and that content used only in structured data and not shown to users is not eligible for the rich result. This tool does not quote the live page text verbatim since that text can change without notice; read the current FAQPage and HowTo structured data guidelines on developers.google.com for the exact current wording, and treat this as the sourced, dated pointer to go read it rather than a substitute for doing so.

Why do AI answer engines make this matter beyond FAQPage and HowTo?

A search engine's rich-result eligibility check is one consumer of JSON-LD. An AI system summarizing or answering questions about a page is another, and it has no equivalent published policy requiring the markup to match what a human sees -- it can simply read the JSON-LD as a structured, pre-parsed statement of what the page says and repeat it. A Product, Review, or Organization block that drifted from the page's actual copy is exactly as capable of misleading a reader that way as a FAQPage block is, even though Google's written rule names only two of the six types this tool checks.

How does the two-lockfile-style diff this tool's siblings use apply to a single page?

It doesn't, directly -- this tool checks one page's JSON-LD against that same page's own visible text, not two point-in-time snapshots against each other. The shared idea with this portfolio's other checkers is the same deterministic, no-network, no-verdict shape: read exactly what is already present, compare two specific things character by character, and report precisely where they part ways rather than issuing an opinion.

No warranty. This page and the tool it documents report whether a JSON-LD claim's exact text is present in the page's own visible copy. Nothing here is SEO, legal, or marketing advice, a Search Console substitute, or a guarantee about rich-result eligibility or rankings. Verify by reading the actual page and Google's current documentation before relying on it. Back to the tool.
